title.rendered: How to Choose a Coffee Grinder

excerpt.rendered: Burr or blade? We compare grinder types for home brewers.

content.rendered:
A burr grinder gives an even grind size, which matters for pour-over and espresso. Blade grinders are cheaper but produce uneven particles.

Budget

Entry-level hand grinders start around the price of two bags of beans.
Use a 1:16 coffee-to-water ratio. Bloom for 30 seconds, then pour in slow circles. Total brew time should land near three minutes.

title.rendered: Storing Coffee Beans So They Stay Fresh

excerpt.rendered: Air, light, heat and moisture are the enemies of fresh beans.

content.rendered: Keep beans in an opaque, airtight container at room temperature. Avoid the fridge: moisture condenses on the beans every time you open it.

title.rendered: Espresso at Home: What You Actually Need

excerpt.rendered: The grinder matters more than the machine.

content.rendered: For espresso, a grinder that adjusts in fine steps matters more than an expensive machine. Dose around 18 grams and aim for a 1:2 ratio.

excerpt.rendered: What the labels mean and how to pick.

content.rendered: Single-origin coffee comes from one farm or region and shows distinct flavours. Blends are built for balance and consistency, which suits milk drinks.

excerpt.rendered: Delivery days, pausing, and changing your beans.

excerpt.rendered: A 12-hour cold brew that keeps for a week.

content.rendered: Use a coarse grind and a 1:8 ratio. Steep in the fridge for 12 hours, then strain. Dilute to taste before serving.
